messages.subject_clean: How to move from CFA (measEq.syntax) to SEM with invariance constraints
messages.body_plain:
> how do I transition from the measurement invariance model to the structural model, given that measEq.syntax is designed for CFA models, and the argument ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016" is not applicable in sem?

The same identification methods are applicable to any SEM, not only to a CFA with exogenous factors.  But note that you can only apply constraints to a factor's residual variance, not marginal variance.  In a CFA, there is no distinction because the factors are exogenous (no predictors, so residual variance is total/marginal variance).

To transition to a structural model from the invariance syntax provided by semTools::measEq.syntax(), you can copy the as.character() output to a syntax file and edit the section ## COMMON-FACTOR COVARIANCES by deleting any (residual) covariances that should not be estimated in your structural model.  Obviously, you also need to add the structural regression paths to the lavaan syntax.

> since parameterization = "theta" is recommended for measurement models with ordinal data

That is only necessary if you wish to evaluate strict invariance.

> should I retain this parameterization when specifying the structural model, or is it advisable to switch to parameterization = "delta" at that stage?

If you are not imposing strict-invariance constraints on indicators' residual variances, then it is arbitrary whether you choose delta or theta parameterization.

Best,

Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Thanks in advance for your suggestions

Hi all,

I have an interesting statistical issue that I am having some difficulties interpreting. Any guidance would be greatly appreciated !!!

I will briefly clarify that X here refers to an exposure, M to a mediator, and Y to an outcome variable. All analyses have been run with lavaan.

My team and I are running many different models where we systematically vary X, M, and Y in a classical mediation.

We are observing that for some X and M pairs, when Y is made to systematically vary but X and M remain constant, Path A coefficients change in magnitude, and statistical significance is lost.

Other Path A terms appear robust when X and M is constant but the Y variable changes.

Furthermore, when M and Y is held constant but X systematically varies, Path B is also at times unstable (ie in coefficient magnitude and statistical significance)

This would ordinarily be unexpected under the assumption that each path estimate should reflect a unique, modular component of the model, but I understand that all Paths are estimated at once in SEM. Even still, this is tricky to interpret. My gut feeling is that I should be narrowing my focus onto Paths which are robust to slight model changes, as they represent effects which are not sensitive to subtle changes in the overall model structure or implied variance-covariance.

This would appear to me to be coherent with some arguments in the literature that effects that only exist under narrow model specifications should be treated as less robust - e.g. for Multiverse Analyses  (Steegen et al., 2016), in which robust results are those which are found consistently across data preprocessing methods; Specification curve analysis argues that models should be robust to changes in model specification; extreme bounds analyses argues that robust paths are those which are consistent while testing for all possible combinations of covariates... but these are not necessarily SEM specific.

Alternatively, one could make the claim that changing certain variables necessarily changes context - that Paths may only appear given certain measurement contexts, and instability does not necessarily imply a lack of robustness - rather, conditionality.

I cannot find any literature on this phenomenon for SEM specifically or how to interpret this and what to do more generally - other than this paper, in which authors trimmed Paths which did not drastically estimation of others, as that would point to an 'unnecessary complication' in the model. (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-021-11364-w).  Thus, paths unstable across model configurations in my study would, according to their rationale, imply a necessary complication, in which I would maybe err on the side of not interpreting the unstable paths.

>From the paper:

We initially included all paths in the model, and conducted a model trimming process: where multiple explanatory variables led to the same endogenous variable (e.g. intervention facilities and collective cleaning both lead to latrine cleanliness), we removed a path where its removal did not alter path coefficients for other explanatory variables and was therefore considered an unnecessary complication.

messages.body_plain:
Structural equation models are systems of equations where model parameters link variables. Language, by contrast, is imprecise and approximate--it leaves gaps that must be filled by the receiver's beliefs, biases and past experience. Describing a system of equations using only language, and not equations, is fraught.
     You write about varying the values of your variables, and observing changes in model parameters. There are many possible reasons, depending on the exact structure of your model. Are you estimating a mean structure for this model, or just the covariance structure? Are you explicitly including error variances in your models, or relying on defaults? Is your structural model saturated, or are you modeling "full mediation," with paths from X to M and from M to Y, but with no direct path from X to Y? Some of your models may be misspecified, depending on choices you have made, and misspecification could induce bias on parameter estimates.
     If you are manipulating values of observed variables and not parameters, then the literature on the impact of unmodeled random  error may be (or may not be) relevant. Your manipulations of X, M and Y may be implicitly inducing changes in random error, which will affect *standardized* parameter estimates but will only affect *unstandardized* parameter estimates sometimes. In particular, random error in the dependent variable, Y, will not affect *unstandardized* regression parameter estimates.
     It may also be that manipu;lations of multiple variables at the same time may create offsetting effects on parameter estimates in some cases. Most variables in a structural equation model are subject to the effects of multiple model parameters, so there is not a struct 1 to 1 between values of variables and values of individual parameters, when the values of *other* parameters are left uncontrolled. Unless the model is completely specified at the level of the parameters, changing the values of the variables can have unpredictable effects.
     Rigdon, E. E. (1994). Demonstrating the effects of unmodeled random measurement error. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 1(4), 375-380.

Thank you both!

I'm working with multiply imputed datasets, and I'm unsure whether the SAM approach can be applied in this context. Additionally, the moderator in my model has many indicators, making it difficult to create product terms between the indicators of two latent IVs and the mediator's indicators, both in the SEM model and in the imputation model.

My questions are as follows:
Can I create a factor score for the moderator (modelled as a second-order factor) and then use those scores (treated as observed variables) to create product terms with the IVs and mediators while one of the IVs has continuous indicators (using parcelling), the other IV has ordinal indicators (coded 0, 1, 2), and the mediator's indicators are binary?

Alternatively, would it be more appropriate to use the first-order latent factors of the moderator (3 factors) to create product terms, i.e., use their factor scores as observed variables? This would significantly increase the number of product terms, but it may allow for interactions between latent variables, while still using observed proxies (factor scores).

The second-order factor score approach simplifies the number of product terms, but it may be problematic to create interaction terms where one variable is a latent construct (with indicators) and the other is a single observed variable (the factor score). I'm not entirely sure whether this mismatch is methodologically acceptable. In contrast, the first-order factor score approach allows for interaction terms between multiple latent constructs by treating their factor scores as observed variables. However, this comes at the cost of increased complexity in both the SEM model and the imputation model.

My main questions are:
Are these approaches acceptable in practice, or are there better alternatives for handling this kind of scenario, especially when working with latent interaction terms, non-continuous indicators, and multiple imputation?

I would greatly appreciate any advice or suggestions on how best to approach this.

Best wishes,
Ahmad

I will go out on a limb a little bit. The drivers of your robust CFI and RMSEA scores are going to be (1) the constraints of your mCFA being inconsistent with the data; (2) the distribution of your data deviating from what one would expect given an underlying multinormal distribution; and (3) sample size. Keep in mind also that expectations for the values of fit indices rely on a certain "typical" model--they are not customized to your model. "Dynamic" fit index thresholds, achieved through simulation, might give you a better basis for evaluating your results.
     Your model is pretty simple and should yield only 4 degrees of freedom. The CFA model only requires that each of the 5 items load only on the assigned factor and that all shared variance across items be mediated by those factors. So less-good fit index values suggest that something else is going on. I can imagine that, with such closely connected psychological constructs, there may be cross-loadings, correlated residual variance or items mis-assigned to factors.
     I notice that your "robust" values for RMSEA and CFI are less good than the original values. Typically, excess kurtosis in data causes robust values to be adjusted to indicate better fit. But if data show the opposite--too little kurtosis versus what would be expected from underlying normality--then the opposite happens. Look at histograms of your data--are they flat or maybe U-shaped, rather than especially peaked? Alternatively, do you have miscoded missing data or careless responses? (I doubt this last one, given the high factor correlation.) That could explain both the lack of fit and the behavior of the robust fit indices.
     As noted above, CFI and RMSEA behave "as expected" only for certain ranges of sample size, given model complexity. Is your sample size especially large or small? Your choice of estimator also relies on very large sample size, so if sample size were small, that would again explain a great deal of what you are seeing.

Michael--
Even with equality of observed variable intercepts and loadings, factor means are not identified in absolute terms.default here is to fix factor means / intercepts to 0 in the first group. Then factor means / intercepts in other groups are identified relative to that 0. You could change which group's parameters are constrained to 0, you could change these constrained values to something other than 0, but you can't escape the arbitrary nature of factor means /. intercepts. That is part of the price of modeling using these imaginary variables. If you were modeling with composites instead of common factors, then these means would be specific functions of the observed variable means and the weights assigned to the observed variables.

messages.body_plain:
Michael--
1.  Check out the lavTestScore() function in the lavaan documentation (use rseek.com <http://rseek.com> if the doc isn't handy). This tool is designed to help in such situations.
2.  If you estimate meanstructure, then you should have intercepts for the common factors (the "alpha" matrix). In a multigroup invariance analysis, these intercepts are fixed to 0 in the first group by default. In general the meanstructure formula for a common factor is:

factor = intercept + b1 * predictor1 + b2 * predictor2 + ... + error

Take expected values:

E(factor) = intercept + b1 * E(predictor1) + b2 * E(predictor2) + ... + E(error)

In a CFA, where there is no structural model, the factors have no predictors, then, assuming E(error) = 0:

E(factor) = mean of factor = intercept

With a structural model, you would fill in the means of the predictor factors to find the mean of your particular factor.

messages.subject_clean: Variance contraints
messages.body_plain:
The creators of lavaan made the choice to standardize the residual variances of the factors rather than standardizing the factors' total variance. Residual variances are parameters of the model, while total variances are not, if the factors are dependent on predictors.
      If you want to force factor total variances to be standardized, you can do that with constraints. If your structural model is:

factor1 = b2 * factor2 + error

then the total variance of factor1 is (assuming predictor and error are orthogonal):

variance (factor1) = b2 squared * variance (factor2) + variance(error)

So if you want the total variance of factor1 to be 1, you can constrain the error variance to be 1 - the variance accounted for by the predictor. So label error variance parameters and specify a constraint:

factor1 ~ b2*factor2
factor1 ~~ a*factor1
factor2 ~~ c*factor2
a == 1 - (b2^2) * c

If factor2 here is itself standardized and without predictors, then its (total) variance is 1, and this code simplifies to:

factor1 ~ b2*factor2
factor1 ~~ a*factor1
a == 1 - b2^2

I would guess that those loadings of 1 are starting values only, not maximum likelihood estimates. Starting values of 1 are plausible, but you could set other starting values using the start() modifier or the ? operator. You could change some starting values are demonstrate for yourself that this is happening.

The output should come with a warning that standard errors could not be estimated and that the model is not statistically identified. The common factor model is inherently not identified without constraints. (Pretty much every statistical model has such required constraints.) To achieve identification for a factor model, the typical approaches are (1) fix one loading per factor to a nonzero value--1 for convenience, (2) fix each factors variance or residual variance to a nonzero value--again, 1 for convenience, or (30 in the "effects coding" approach, constrain the average loading for each factor to 1.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’m testing measurement invariance over time (years) using lavaan.
My data consist of ordinal Likert-type items (1–4) measuring a single-factor construct, and I follow the approach recommended by Rutkowski & Svetina.

According to their guidelines for ordinal data with one factor:

For metric invariance, invariance is supported when:
ΔRMSEA ≤ .05 in conjunction with significant Δχ² and ΔCFI ≥ –.004

For scalar invariance, invariance is supported when:
ΔRMSEA ≤ .01 in conjunction with significant Δχ² and ΔCFI ≥ –.004

They use compareFit() (from semTools) to compare nested models.
However, to specifically test whether the chi-squared difference between models is significant, I’m using:

lavTestLRT(fit.baseline, fit.prop4)

 Is this correct ?

Thanks in advance for your help!

messages.subject: RI CLPM 2groups 5time points
messages.subject_clean: RI CLPM 2groups 5time points
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

I would appreciate your feedback and advice on the specification of the RI CLPM for 2 groups.

I have two groups of MZ and DZ twins (~1000 individuals in each group) measured more than 5 times for two phenotypes: subjective health (she) and life satisfaction (gls). I want to examine the cross-lagged associations across time for these two groups.

I have to take into account that 1) data is clustered 2) MZ and DZ twins can have different loadings 3) there are also control variables.

What I struggle with:
The model stops converging after adding the fourth time point. I believe this is due to model complexity and small sample size. Currently, I am thinking of running separate models for timepoints (tp) 1, 2, and 3, and then a separate model for tp 2, 3, and 4.  Is this solution feasible? Should I then "just" specify estimated loadings and intercepts from the model with tp 1,2,3 as starting values (or just values) in the model with tp 2,3, and 4?
The model stops converging when I have restrictions for the control variables (sex, age, etc. ) to set the error to zero. It feels that with two groups and control variables, we should have enough pieces of information to measure the model even without this restriction; therefore, I removed it. Does it make sense?
Do I understand correctly that specification of the model within 2 groups will allow me to run the analysis keeping 2 separate variance-covariance matrices? If I have more degrees of freedom in one group (more restrictions), can this information be used to estimate the parameters in the model with fewer degrees of freedom in another group?
Allowing different intercepts across groups. I can specify the different loadings for the regressive pathways for two phenotypes, but I struggle to set different intercepts, as they are all restricted to make the model identifiable.

model:

riclpm_3tp <- '

# Define intercept factors
i_gls =~ 1*gls_lv_ad_1+1*gls_lv_ad_2+1*gls_lv_ad_3
i_she =~ 1*she0100_comb_1+1*she0100_comb_2+1*she0100_comb_3

i_gls ~ sex + age0100_scaled_1

# Define single item latent variables
eta_gls1 =~ 1*gls_lv_ad_1+urbanicity_scaled_1+yeduc_scaled_1+hh_inc_scaled_1
eta_gls2 =~ 1*gls_lv_ad_2+urbanicity_scaled_2+yeduc_scaled_2+hh_inc_scaled_2
eta_gls3 =~ 1*gls_lv_ad_3+urbanicity_scaled_3+yeduc_scaled_3+hh_inc_scaled_3

eta_she1 =~ 1*she0100_comb_1
eta_she2 =~ 1*she0100_comb_2
eta_she3 =~ 1*she0100_comb_3

# Autoregressive effects
eta_gls2 ~ c(a1,a2)*eta_gls1
eta_gls3 ~ c(a1,a2)*eta_gls2

eta_she2 ~ c(a1,a2)*eta_she1
eta_she3 ~ c(a1,a2)*eta_she2

# Crosslagged effects

eta_she2 ~ c(m1,m2)*eta_gls1 #start(c(1.2, 0.6))
eta_she3 ~ c(m1,m2)*eta_gls2

eta_gls2 ~ c(m1,m2)*eta_she1
eta_gls3 ~ c(m1,m2)*eta_she2

# Some further constraints on the variance structure

# 1. Set error variances of the observed variables to zero
gls_lv_ad_1 ~~ 0*gls_lv_ad_1
gls_lv_ad_2 ~~ 0*gls_lv_ad_2
gls_lv_ad_3 ~~ 0*gls_lv_ad_3

she0100_comb_1 ~~ 0*she0100_comb_1
she0100_comb_2 ~~ 0*she0100_comb_2
she0100_comb_3 ~~ 0*she0100_comb_3

# 2. Let lavaan estimate the variance of the latent variables
eta_gls1 ~~ vargls1*eta_gls1
eta_gls2 ~~ vargls2*eta_gls2
eta_gls3 ~~ vargls3*eta_gls3

eta_she1 ~~ varshe1*eta_she1
eta_she2 ~~ varshe2*eta_she2
eta_she3 ~~ varshe3*eta_she3

# 3. We also want estimates of the intercept factor variances and an
#    estimate of their covariance
i_gls ~~ varigls*i_gls
i_she ~~ varishe*i_she
i_gls ~~ covi*i_she

# 4. We have to define that the covariance between the intercepts and
#    the latents of the first time point are zero

eta_gls1 ~~ 0*i_gls
eta_she1 ~~ 0*i_gls
eta_gls1 ~~ 0*i_she
eta_she1 ~~ 0*i_she

# 5. Finally, we estimate the covariance between the latents of x and y
#    of the first time point, the second time-point and so on. note that
#    for the second to fourth time point the correlation is constrained to
#    the same value

eta_gls1 ~~ cov1*eta_she1
eta_gls2 ~~ e1*eta_she2
eta_gls3 ~~ e1*eta_she3

# The model also contains a mean structure and we have to define some
# constraints for this part of the model. the assumption is that we
# only want estimates of the mean of the intercept factors. all other means
# are defined to be zero:
gls_lv_ad_1 ~ 0*1
gls_lv_ad_2 ~ 0*1
gls_lv_ad_3 ~ 0*1

she0100_comb_1 ~ 0*1
she0100_comb_2 ~ 0*1
she0100_comb_3 ~ 0*1

sex ~ 0.5*1
age0100_scaled_1 ~ 0*1

urbanicity_scaled_1 ~ 0*1
urbanicity_scaled_2 ~ 0*1
urbanicity_scaled_3 ~ 0*1

yeduc_scaled_1 ~ 0*1
yeduc_scaled_2 ~ 0*1
yeduc_scaled_3 ~ 0*1

hh_inc_scaled_1 ~ 0*1
hh_inc_scaled_2 ~ 0*1
hh_inc_scaled_3 ~ 0*1

eta_gls1 ~ 1
eta_gls2 ~ 1
eta_gls3 ~ 1

eta_she1 ~ 1
eta_she2 ~ 1
eta_she3 ~ 1

i_gls ~ 1
i_she ~ 1

## define correlations
cori := covi / (sqrt(varigls) * sqrt(varishe))
cor1 := cov1 / (sqrt(vargls1) * sqrt(varshe1))
cort2 := e1 / (sqrt(vargls2) * sqrt(varshe2))
cort3 := e1 / (sqrt(vargls3) * sqrt(varshe3))
'

riclpm_fit<- sem(riclpm_3tp, cluster = "fid", group = "zyg",data=df,mimic = "Mplus", missing = "FIML")

thank you in advance!

This issue has been around for a while. When using Wald tests, both parameter estimates and standard errors (and thus p-values) can change based on how you set the scale of a latent variable (with std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE you are fixing latent variances to 1 with std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE you are fixing the first factor loading to 1). Gonzalez & Griffin (2001) do a nice job talking about this issue: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11570231/

One additional note: model fit should be the same for both models so if you want a method of testing parameters that's not affected by how you set the scale nested model tests of parameters (likelihood ratio tests) avoid this issue.

Alex

This is a post to the follwoing discussion:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Nam3N7Y4b78/m/KdW-Oyo3AQAJ

This issue is an interesting one, raised a long time ago, but rarely discussed in the application of SEM. This is another related paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

The p-values reported by many SEM programs are, by default, the Wald p-values, which are not invariant to the parameterization of the model. The likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a., chi-square difference test) p-value may be what we usually "really" want: If we fix a parameter to zero, is the model fit significantly different from the original model? This test yields the same p-value whether we fix a factor loading to one or fix the factor variances to one.

One obvious drawback of the LRT p-values is the computational cost. For Wald p-values, we don't have to fit another model. For LRT p-values, we need to fit one more model for each parameter.

To try making LRT p-values more accessible and address the issue with the Wald p-value, Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp. This is a demonstration of how to use it:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is basically this:

For each free parameter with the LRT p-value requested:
- Fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero.
- Do the LRT.
- Report the p-value.

This is demonstration using a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"

Two models are fitted, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one:

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

As expected, these two models have identical goodness of fit:

# Compare model fit
fit_v1

#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB

#>   Degrees of freedom                                51

#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML

#>
#> Model Test User Model:

#>   Test statistic                                63.442
#>   Degrees of freedom                                51

However, the p-values of free parameters can be different, sometimes non-negligibly, unless they are very small (e.g., p < .001).

# Compare the Wald p-values
parameterEstimates(fit_v1,
                   ci = FALSE,
                   output = "text")[c(1:12, 28:30), ]
#>
#> Latent Variables:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

#>     f3                0.252    0.104    2.413    0.016
parameterEstimates(fit_v2,
                   ci = FALSE,
                   output = "text")[c(1:12, 28:30), ]
#>

#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>   f1 =~

The function lrtp() can be used to compute the LRT p-values. By default, it only computes LRT p-values for regression coefficients ("~") and covariances ("~~", error variances and variances are excluded), to save computational cost. #>     f3                0.252    0.104   10.540    0.001
fit_v2_lrtp
#>
#> Parameter Estimates:
#>
#>   Standard errors                             Standard
#>   Information                                 Expected
#>   Information saturated (h1) model          Structured
#>
#> Latent Variables:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err    Chisq     LRTp
#>   f1 =~
#>     x1                0.375    0.136    7.134    0.008
#>     x2                0.313    0.144    4.566    0.033
#>     x3                0.699    0.162   18.416    0.000
#>     x4                0.323    0.150    4.450    0.035
#>   f2 =~
#>     x5                0.510    0.141   11.804    0.001
#>     x6                0.524    0.146   11.052    0.001
#>     x7                0.528    0.147   11.121    0.001

#>   f3 =~
#>     x9                0.929    0.137   39.408    0.000
#>     x10               0.701    0.136   24.355    0.000
#>     x11               0.831    0.125   37.789    0.000
#>     x12               0.579    0.126   19.562    0.000
#>
#> Covariances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err    Chisq     LRTp
#>   f1 ~~
#>     f2                0.470    0.184    5.563    0.018
#>     f3                0.593    0.147   12.189    0.000
#>   f2 ~~
#>     f3                0.531    0.141   10.540    0.001

Not demonstrated above, the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choices of the items with their loadings fixed to one.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the packages, we found cases in which the computation failed, because the model with a parameter fixed to zero failed to converge or had Heywood cases. We are working on this.

In any case, the function just does what we can do manually. Therefore, for these "difficult parameters," if we want to have the LRT p-values, we can fit the model manually and tweak some settings, such as the bounds.

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

-- Shu Fai

For the indirect effect in a mediation model, if you use bootstrapping, whethe you fix the loading to one or fix the factor variances to one should not matter, usually.

This can be demonstrated for the standardized indirect effect. It is a known characteristic of the standardized coefficients that they are the same whether we fix the first loadings or the factor variances to one (assuming single sample model and no equality constraints). So, for each bootstrap sample, the standardized indirect effect is the same whether we fix the loadings or the factor variances. The p-values in each bootstrap sample are irrelevant. Therefore, the bootstrap CI will also be the same.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
This issue is an interesting one, raised a long time ago, but rarely discussed in the application of SEM. This is another related paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

The p-values reported by many SEM programs are, by default, the Wald p-values, which are not invariant to the parameterization of the model. The likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a., chi-square difference test) p-value may be what we usually "really" want: If we fix a parameter to zero, is the model fit significantly different from the original model? This test yields the same p-value whether we fix a factor loading to one or fix the factor variances to one.

One obvious drawback of the LRT p-values is the computational cost. For Wald p-values, we don't have to fit another model. For LRT p-values, we need to fit one more model for each parameter.

To try making LRT p-values more accessible and address the issue with the Wald p-value, Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp. This is a demonstration of how to use it:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is basically this:

For each free parameter with the LRT p-value requested:
- Fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero.
- Do the LRT.
- Report the p-value.

This is demonstration using a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"

Two models are fitted, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one:

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

As expected, these two models have identical goodness of fit:

# Compare model fit
fit_v1

                   ci = FALSE,

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

messages.body_plain:
This issue is an interesting one, raised a long time ago, but rarely discussed in the application of SEM. This is another related paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

The p-values reported by many SEM programs are, by default, the Wald p-values, which are not invariant to the parameterization of the model. The likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a., chi-square difference test) p-value may be what we usually "really" want: If we fix a parameter to zero, is the model fit significantly different from the original model? This test yields the same p-value whether we fix a factor loading to one or fix the factor variances to one.

One obvious drawback of the LRT p-values is the computational cost. For Wald p-values, we don't have to fit another model. For LRT p-values, we need to fit one more model for each parameter.

To try making LRT p-values more accessible and address the issue with the Wald p-value, Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp. This is a demonstration of how to use it:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is basically this:

For each free parameter with the LRT p-value requested:
- Fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero.
- Do the LRT.
- Report the p-value.

This is demonstration using a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"

Two models are fitted, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one:

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

As expected, these two models have identical goodness of fit:

# Compare model fit
fit_v1
#> lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 52 iterations
#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                        27
#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                63.442
#>   Degrees of freedom                                51
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.113
fit_v2

#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                        27
#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                63.442
#>   Degrees of freedom                                51
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.113

However, the p-values of free parameters can be different, sometimes non-negligibly, unless they are very small (e.g., p < .001).

# Compare the Wald p-values
parameterEstimates(fit_v1,
                   ci = FALSE,
                   output = "text")[c(1:12, 28:30), ]
#>
#> Latent Variables:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>   f1 =~
#>     x1                1.000
#>     x2                0.834    0.482    1.733    0.083

#>   f1 ~~

#>   f2 ~~
#>     f3                0.252    0.104    2.413    0.016
parameterEstimates(fit_v2,
                   ci = FALSE,
                   output = "text")[c(1:12, 28:30), ]

#>     x11               0.831    0.125   37.789    0.000
#>     x12               0.579    0.126   19.562    0.000
#>
#> Covariances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err    Chisq     LRTp
#>   f1 ~~

#>   f2 ~~

Not demonstrated above, the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choices of the items with their loadings fixed to one.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the packages, we found cases in which the computation failed, because the model with a parameter fixed to zero failed to converge or had Heywood cases. We are working on this.

In any case, the function just does what we can do manually. Therefore, for these "difficult parameters," if we want to have the LRT p-values, we can fit the model manually and tweak some settings, such as the bounds.

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

-- Shu Fai

Hi,

After establishing measurement invariance, I would like to compare the direct and indirect paths among four groups. However, I’m a bit confused about which tests to use when comparing paths in SEM across more than two groups: lavTestLRT() or lavTestWald().

It’s much simpler when comparing only two groups, where we typically use lavTestLRT() to assess differences in model fit. But as the number of groups increases, it becomes more complex to impose and release constraints and compare the models using lavTestLRT().

What is the best practice—or the most commonly recommended approach, for comparing structural paths across more than two groups in this context?

It is worth mentioning that I used both approaches and I got different results: lavTestLRT showed an overall difference between groups while pairwise lavTestWald showed no significant differences between groups.
Best,
Ahmad

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am very new to MI so these questions may seem basic.

I conducted cross-regional (United Kingdom versus Hong Kong China) measurement invariance tests w Lavaan. I have the following questions:
1) For the DV (which only consists of 3 items, about behavioral intentions), w MGCFA, I found evidence for metric invariance but not scalar invariance. Is it worthwhile to run measurement invariance for a scale with only 3 items? Any papers regarding this issue?
2) Given that we found no support for scale invariance, is it okay to run multiple regressions that includes message framing as IV (gain versus nonloss framing), region*message framing as an interaction term (region as a potential moderator), plus another covariate, with behavioral intentions as the DV (in which there is support for metric invariance but not scalar invariance) I know the means in behavioral intentions between regions cannot be compared well, so I won't interpret the region term of the regression. But is it methodologically sound to test the interaction (region*message framing)?
3) I also included individual difference moderators (e.g. regulatory focus). Again, I found support for metric invariance but not scalar invariance with a regulatory focus scale (Vriend et al., 2022). Let's say I run another regression with message framing as IV, region as another term (I won't interpret the group differences), a covariate, regulatory focus, and interaction term of message framing*regulatory focus, with the same DV (behavioral intentions). Is it okay to combine both the UK and HK samples in the regression analyses while focusing on testing the individual difference moderation (message framing*regulatory focus)? Or should I separate HK and UK samples in running such analyses?

Will appreciate if there are academic papers/references so that I can read more, thank you!

Regards,
Kit

     The warning (not error) message just says that some of your bootstrap replications produced unacceptable values for some parameter estimates, most likely some negative error variances.. If the population values for these residual variances are close to 0, then across enough replications you will get some estimates that are less than zero, purely as a matter of random sampling variance. You should still have all results available. Ken Bollen wrote a paper on this topic, suggesting that negative residual variances due to random sampling error could be safely ignored. If these negative residual variances are a problem,  you could add an inequality constraint to your model,m specifying that residual variances involved must be greater than 0.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm performing measurement invariance testing across six groups using lavaan with categorical data (4-point Likert), the WLSMV estimator, and the delta parameterization with Wu & Estabrook (2016) identification, following the procedure outlined in Svetina et al. (2019).

I am testing:

Configural invariance

Thresholds invariance

Thresholds + loadings invariance

I use measEq.syntax() from the semTools package and compare models using both fitmeasures() (for ΔCFI and ΔRMSEA) and lavTestLRT() (for Δχ², Satorra-Bentler scaled).

In Svetina et al. (2019), I found this statement:

> “Metric invariance is supported when ΔRMSEA ≤ 0.01 in conjuction with sig chi-square difference test and  ΔCFI ≥ –.004 for metric".

>
> In other words, this means that even if the chi-square difference test is significant (p < 0.05), but ΔCFI and ΔRMSEA stay within acceptable thresholds , metric invariance can be considered supported?

messages.subject: Re: WLSMV for latent moderated SEM using product terms?
messages.subject_clean: WLSMV for latent moderated SEM using product terms?
messages.body_plain:
> Is the WLSMV estimator suitable for latent moderated SEM using product terms (i.e., continuous indicators × binary/ordinal indicators)?

Generally, no.  Because you cannot calculate a product with a latent response underlying an ordinal indicator, the product indicator approach is only available if you are willing to treat the ordinal indicators as continuous (i.e., treating whatever arbitrary numerical weights you assign to each category as though they were real numbers).

A somewhat arbitrary exception could be made for a single dichotomous variable, representing groups across which you want to test invariance.

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1151-3

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-77249-3_20

But I don't think this is the situation you are thinking of.

Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Dear lavaan community,

I have a question regarding the correlation between a residual variance and an external, manifest variable.

In our model, all manifest variables are dichotomous. We created pseudo-latent factors for the residuals and correlate these with a dichotomous manifest variable. We use WLSMV and theta parameterization. If I understand CFA for binary indicators correctly, the residual variance is expected to be approximately normally distributed.

My question is: what type of correlation gets calculated in lavaan for the continuous latent residual and the dichotomous manifest variable? Is it a biserial correlation, as would be expected with two manifest variables?

Thank you in advance,

Johanna

f =~ a_1 + a_2 + a_4 + b_1 + b_3 + b_4

f ~~ 1*f
